STATE CIVIL SERVICE APPOINTMENT: MERIT EXAMINATIONS, ELIGIBLE LISTS, CERTIFICATION, AND PROBATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Associate Governmental Program Analyst

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — APPOINTMENT TO A POSITION IN THE CALIFORNIA STATE CIVIL SERVICE
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with the class Associate Governmental Program Analyst and the appointing agency California Department of Example Services. This information sheet describes how California law fills positions in the state civil service: the constitutional merit mandate in Article VII of the California Constitution, the examination and eligible-list provisions of the State Civil Service Act (Government Code sections 18900 and following), the certification and appointment provisions of that Act (sections 19050 and following), the veterans' preference article, the rules on temporary appointment, the probationary period, and the case law on what happens when an appointment is made contrary to those provisions. It describes hiring and appointment only. It is not an employment application, an examination application, a request for veterans' preference, an appeal to the State Personnel Board or the Department of Human Resources, a petition for writ of mandate, or a court filing, and completing it does not create, preserve, extend, or waive any deadline, eligibility, rank, or appeal right under Article VII, under the State Civil Service Act, under a board rule, or under a memorandum of understanding. Completing it does not establish that California Department of Example Services did or did not take any action described in this sheet, or that any statement in it is true of any particular examination, list, or appointment.

THE CONSTITUTIONAL SOURCE: ARTICLE VII'S DEFINITION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE AND ITS MERIT-AND-COMPETITIVE-EXAMINATION COMMAND
Hiring into the California state civil service begins with a provision of the state Constitution rather than with a statute. Article VII, section 1 does two things in two subdivisions. Subdivision (a) fixes the scope of the civil service by defining it to include every state officer and employee except as the Constitution itself provides otherwise. Subdivision (b) fixes the method by which the positions inside that scope are filled: permanent appointment, and promotion, are to be made under a general system based on merit ascertained by competitive examination. The California Supreme Court reproduced subdivision (b) in Professional Engineers v. Department of Transportation and there described the State Civil Service Act, Government Code section 18500 and following, as the legislation implementing Article VII. In the same passage the court recited the ballot argument presented to the voters when the predecessor provision, former article XXIV, was adopted in 1934, which stated the purpose of the civil service provision in terms of barring appointment and promotion in the service except on the basis of merit, efficiency, and fitness ascertained by competitive examination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]

  — Cal. Const., art. VII, § 1(a) (California Legislative Information text; independently confirmed on onecle), Cal. Const., art. VII, § 1, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=VII)
  "civil service permanent appointment and promotion shall be made under a general system based on merit ascertained by competitive examination"
  — Cal. Const., art. VII, § 1(b) (California Legislative Information text; independently confirmed on onecle and reproduced by the Supreme Court in Professional Engineers v. Department of Transportation), Cal. Const., art. VII, § 1, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=VII)
  "appointments and promotion in the service except on the basis of merit, efficiency, and fitness ascertained by competitive examination"
  — Professional Engineers v. Department of Transportation (1997) 15 Cal.4th 543, 15 Cal.4th at p. 548 (quoting the 1934 ballot argument as recited in State Compensation Ins. Fund v. Riley (1937) 9 Cal.2d 126, 134) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1224847/professional-engineers-v-department-of-transportation/)
  Known gap: Article VII, section 1 states the merit command in general terms and does not itself define "competitive examination," identify which positions are permanent, or say how an examination is to be constructed, scored, or ranked; those subjects are addressed by the statutes and the board rules described in the clauses that follow, not by the constitutional text quoted here. This clause also does not address Article VII, section 4, which lists the categories of state officers and employees exempt from the civil service (among them University of California and California State University personnel and the employees of elected officers), so nothing here establishes that any particular position is inside the civil service at all. Verification: the constitutional text was fetched from two genuinely independent publishers, the Legislative Counsel's California Legislative Information site and onecle's California Constitution pages, and the quoted words are a verbatim substring of both; onecle's copy is hard-wrapped, so the comparison was made after collapsing runs of whitespace, which is the only normalization applied. The Professional Engineers quotation was available from only one free publisher; CourtListener's Official Reports text is the single reachable copy, no courts.ca.gov slip PDF exists for a 1997 opinion (a request for S049151 returned 404), and Justia, FindLaw, Google Scholar, casetext and case.law are unreachable from this environment, so "verified" for that opinion means verified against one publication, cross-checked by an exact-phrase index query on its cluster (count 1), and not corroborated by a second publisher. Two defects in that single publication are disclosed rather than corrected: the court renders the constitutional clause with a bracketed lower-case initial, "[i]n the civil service permanent appointment ...", so the quote below begins after the bracketed letter and does not reproduce the capital "I" that the Constitution itself prints; and in the ballot-argument sentence CourtListener's text prints "prohibiting]" with a closing bracket but no opening bracket, which is an artifact of that scan, so the quote below begins after that word rather than reproducing it. The page 548 pin cites were read off star pagination that runs monotonically through the majority opinion; the only non-monotonic markers in that document appear far later, in the separate opinions, well past the quoted passages.

THE STATE CIVIL SERVICE ACT'S OWN STATEMENT OF PURPOSE, INCLUDING ITS APPLICANT-FACING NONDISCRIMINATION CLAUSE
The State Civil Service Act opens with a purpose section that states, in the Legislature's own words, what the Act is for. Government Code section 18500 says the purpose of the part is to facilitate the operation of Article VII, to promote economy and efficiency in the state service, and to provide a comprehensive personnel system in which several enumerated things are true. Two of those enumerated items bear directly on hiring. One states that appointments are based upon merit and fitness ascertained through practical and competitive examination. Another is addressed to applicants as well as employees, and states that applicants and employees are treated in an equitable manner without regard to a list of characteristics and to non-job-related factors. This statutory list is the Act's own internal nondiscrimination statement; it sits alongside, and does not replace, the Fair Employment and Housing Act and the other statutes this corpus addresses in separate documents.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-14]
  "Appointments are based upon merit and fitness ascertained through practical and competitive examination."
  — Cal. Gov.   "Applicants and employees are treated in an equitable manner without regard to political affiliation, race, color, sex, religious creed, national origin, ancestry, marital status, age, sexual orientation, disability, political or religious opinions or nonjob-related factors."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 18500(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text; independently confirmed on onecle), purpose of the State Civil Service Act — equitable treatment of applicants and employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=18500.)
  Known gap: Section 18500 is a declaration of purpose. This clause does not address whether that section creates a private right of action, supplies a cause of action independent of the Fair Employment and Housing Act, or is enforced only through the State Personnel Board and the Department of Human Resources; no case law on that question is cited or relied on here, and the clause makes no claim about it. The characteristics enumerated in subdivision (c)(5) as quoted are those the section itself lists; that list is not identical to the protected characteristics enumerated in Government Code section 12940, and this clause does not reconcile the two or suggest that either list controls the other. Neither quote below spans a cross-reference. The only normalization applied was collapsing runs of whitespace and converting typographic quotation marks.

HOW AN ELIGIBLE LIST IS CREATED: FREE COMPETITIVE EXAMINATIONS, MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS, AND THE PERMITTED FORMS OF EXAMINATION
The statutory route into a state civil service position runs through an eligible list, and the list is a product of examination. Government Code section 18900 provides that eligible lists are established as the result of free competitive examinations, open to persons who lawfully may be appointed to a position within the class and who meet the minimum qualifications prescribed by the class specification or by rule; the same section permits the department to limit the size of candidate groups in entry-level and nonpromotional examinations in stated circumstances. Government Code section 18930 states the standard the examination itself must satisfy — it must be competitive, and of such a character as fairly to test and determine the qualifications, fitness, and ability of competitors actually to perform the duties of the class. The same section describes the permissible forms an examination may take, which are not limited to a written test: an examination may be assembled or unassembled, written or oral, or a demonstration of skill, or a combination, and the section lists investigations of character, personality, education and experience, and tests of intelligence, capacity, technical knowledge, manual skill, and physical fitness among the devices that may be employed. Section 18930 also contains a separate open-basis rule for managerial positions, with exceptions for career executive assignments, certain peace officers, and two named forestry classes.

  — Cal. Gov. Code § 18900(a) (California Legislative Information text; independently confirmed on onecle), establishment of eligible lists by free competitive examination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=18900.)

It does not address the Limited Examination and Appointment Program for applicants with disabilities, career executive assignments, or the class-by-class examination plans, bulletins, and board rules that determine what a particular examination actually consists of, how it is weighted, and what minimum qualifications a particular class specification imposes; those are found in materials outside the statutes quoted here. Nothing in this clause addresses whether a particular selection device described in section 18930 — a personality investigation, a physical fitness test, or a medical or psychological screen — is independently limited by the Fair Employment and Housing Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the constitutional right of privacy, or the statutes this corpus covers in its separate documents on pre-employment medical examinations, physical ability testing, polygraph prohibitions, and automated decision-making; section 18930 authorizes the form of examination and says nothing about those external limits. GROUNDS ON WHICH AN APPLICANT MAY BE REFUSED EXAMINATION OR REMOVED FROM AN ELIGIBLE LIST BEFORE APPOINTMENT
Government Code section 18935 gives the department, or a designated appointing power, three related powers exercisable at different points in the selection process: to refuse to examine an applicant, to refuse after examination to declare the applicant eligible, and to withhold or withdraw a name from an eligible list before the appointment. The section then enumerates the criteria that may support any of those actions. They are lacking a requirement for the examination or the position applied for; having been dismissed from any position for a cause that would be cause for dismissal from state service; having resigned from a position not in good standing in order to avoid dismissal; having misrepresented oneself in the application or examination process, which the statute expressly defines to include permitting another person to complete or attempt to complete a portion of the examination on the applicant's behalf; and having been found unsuited or not qualified for employment pursuant to rule. Subdivision (b) states that these remedies are not exclusive and do not prevent the board, department, or appointing power from taking additional action under the chapter beginning at section 19680.

Nothing here addresses how section 18935 interacts with the separate California statutes restricting an employer's use of criminal history, arrest and diversion records, credit reports, or consumer reports, which this corpus covers in other documents; section 18935 is a civil service eligibility provision and is not a grant of permission under those statutes. APPOINTMENT FROM EMPLOYMENT LISTS, AND THE CERTIFICATION OF THE THREE HIGHEST RANKS
Government Code section 19050 states the general command that governs a state appointing power: in all cases not excepted or exempted by virtue of Article VII, it is to fill positions by appointment — including transfers, reinstatements, promotions, and demotions — in strict accordance with the State Civil Service Act and the rules made under it, and not otherwise; and, except as the part provides, appointments to vacant positions are to be made from employment lists. Section 19057.1 describes what the appointing power receives when it moves to fill a vacancy from an employment list. Apart from reemployment lists and State Restriction of Appointment lists, the department provides a certified list of the names and addresses of all eligibles whose scores at the time of certification represent the three highest ranks on the list and who have indicated a willingness to accept appointment on the conditions specified. The statute defines the unit being counted: a rank consists of one or more eligibles with the same whole percentage score, scores being rounded to the nearest whole percent, so a single rank may contain several candidates. The section also provides what happens when the list yields fewer than three ranks, permits the department to certify more or fewer than three ranks when the certified group is disproportionate to the number of vacancies, and contains a separate subdivision (b) alternative list procedure and a subdivision (d) rule for Department of the California Highway Patrol peace officer classes. A different section, 19056, provides that where the appointment is to be made from a departmental or subdivisional reemployment list, the person standing highest is certified and appointed.

VETERANS' PREFERENCE IN ENTRANCE EXAMINATIONS: PLACEMENT IN THE TOP RANK, AND THE LIMITS ON WHO MAY CLAIM IT
Article VII, section 6, subdivision (a) of the California Constitution authorizes the Legislature to provide preferences for veterans and their surviving spouses. The Legislature has done so in a dedicated article of the State Civil Service Act. Government Code section 18973.1 provides the operative mechanism: when a veteran, the widow or widower of a veteran, or the spouse of a 100 percent disabled veteran achieves a passing score on an entrance examination, that person is ranked in the top rank of the resulting eligibility list; the section does not apply to a veteran who has been dishonorably discharged or released. Because certification under section 19057.1 works by ranks rather than by individual scores, placement in the top rank is what makes the preference operate. Section 18973.5 supplies two definitional limits: for purposes of the article an entrance examination is any open competitive examination, and no veterans' preference under the article is awarded to permanent civil service employees. Related sections in the same article credit qualifying military service as experience and address how and when proof of eligibility is submitted.

Nothing here states how a preference claim is filed or what proof is required; section 18976 addresses that and is not quoted. TEMPORARY APPOINTMENT WHEN THERE IS NO EMPLOYMENT LIST, AND THE CONSTITUTIONAL NINE-MONTH CEILING
The merit system contemplates that a position may need to be filled before an eligible list exists, and both the Constitution and the statute address that situation with an express time limit. Article VII, section 5 permits a temporary appointment to a position for which there is no employment list, and then caps it: no person may serve in one or more positions under temporary appointment longer than nine months in twelve consecutive months. Government Code section 19058 implements that provision. It permits the appointing power, with the consent of the department, to fill a position by temporary appointment when there is no employment list from which the position may be filled; it provides that a temporary appointment to a permanent position continues only until eligibles are available from an appropriate employment list and may not exceed the period prescribed by Article VII, section 5; it allows a temporary appointment to a limited-term position to continue for the life of that position within that constitutional period, in the appointing power's discretion and with the department's approval; and it directs that when temporary appointments are made to permanent positions, an appropriate employment list is to be established for each class before the appointment expires.

THE PROBATIONARY PERIOD AS THE FINAL PHASE OF SELECTION, AND THE GROUNDS FOR REJECTION DURING IT
In the state civil service the probationary period is treated as part of the selection process rather than as a separate post-hire event. Government Code section 19170 directs the board to establish the length of the probationary period for each class at six months unless it establishes a longer period of not more than one year, and states when the period commences — on the first day the employee reports to work or begins performing the job duties. The same section permits the board by rule to extend individual probationary periods for time the probationer is absent, and to require an additional probationary period when a probationer returns after an extended absence and the remainder of the period is insufficient to evaluate current performance. Subdivision (c) provides a separate, agreement-based extension of up to six months, subject to board approval, where an employee alleges a disability as defined in Government Code section 12926, so that the appointing power may provide a reasonable accommodation and the employee may demonstrate before the period ends the ability to perform the essential functions with that accommodation; the subdivision states that it relieves no one of other accommodation or antidiscrimination obligations and that no employee may be required to waive such rights as a condition of the extension. Government Code section 19173 states the grounds on which a probationer may be rejected during the period — reasons relating to the probationer's qualifications, the good of the service, or failure to demonstrate merit, efficiency, fitness, and moral responsibility — and provides that the probationer may not be rejected for any cause constituting prohibited discrimination as set forth in sections 19700 to 19703. Subdivision (b) prescribes the written notice of rejection, its contents, an effective date no later than the last day of the probationary period, and a filing with the board within fifteen days after that date.

WHEN AN APPOINTMENT IS MADE CONTRARY TO THE CIVIL SERVICE LAWS: FERDIG V. STATE PERSONNEL BOARD
Ferdig v. State Personnel Board is a California Supreme Court decision about an appointment that was made after the appointee was placed in the certified group by a credit he was never entitled to. The appointee passed a Chief Engineer II examination and was ranked sixteenth. He then applied for a veterans' preference on the strength of a discharge document; the Department of Veterans Affairs advised the State Personnel Board that preference points applied, which moved him to fourth, and a waiver by a candidate ahead of him brought him into the top three and so within the group eligible for appointment. He was appointed. The preference was later determined to have been approved erroneously, because his service did not satisfy the statutory service requirement. expectedJSON.body: Article VII, section 6, subdivision (a) of the California Constitution authorizes the Legislature to provide preferences for veterans and their surviving spouses. The Legislature has done so in a dedicated article of the State Civil Service Act. Government Code section 18973.1 provides the operative mechanism: when a veteran, the widow or widower of a veteran, or the spouse of a 100 percent disabled veteran achieves a passing score on an entrance examination, that person is ranked in the top rank of the resulting eligibility list; the section does not apply to a veteran who has been dishonorably discharged or released. Because certification under section 19057.1 works by ranks rather than by individual scores, placement in the top rank is what makes the preference operate. Section 18973.5 supplies two definitional limits: for purposes of the article an entrance examination is any open competitive examination, and no veterans' preference under the article is awarded to permanent civil service employees. Related sections in the same article credit qualifying military service as experience and address how and when proof of eligibility is submitted.

expectedJSON.body: The merit system contemplates that a position may need to be filled before an eligible list exists, and both the Constitution and the statute address that situation with an express time limit. Article VII, section 5 permits a temporary appointment to a position for which there is no employment list, and then caps it: no person may serve in one or more positions under temporary appointment longer than nine months in twelve consecutive months. Government Code section 19058 implements that provision. It permits the appointing power, with the consent of the department, to fill a position by temporary appointment when there is no employment list from which the position may be filled; it provides that a temporary appointment to a permanent position continues only until eligibles are available from an appropriate employment list and may not exceed the period prescribed by Article VII, section 5; it allows a temporary appointment to a limited-term position to continue for the life of that position within that constitutional period, in the appointing power's discretion and with the department's approval; and it directs that when temporary appointments are made to permanent positions, an appropriate employment list is to be established for each class before the appointment expires.

expectedJSON.body: In the state civil service the probationary period is treated as part of the selection process rather than as a separate post-hire event. Government Code section 19170 directs the board to establish the length of the probationary period for each class at six months unless it establishes a longer period of not more than one year, and states when the period commences — on the first day the employee reports to work or begins performing the job duties. The same section permits the board by rule to extend individual probationary periods for time the probationer is absent, and to require an additional probationary period when a probationer returns after an extended absence and the remainder of the period is insufficient to evaluate current performance. Subdivision (c) provides a separate, agreement-based extension of up to six months, subject to board approval, where an employee alleges a disability as defined in Government Code section 12926, so that the appointing power may provide a reasonable accommodation and the employee may demonstrate before the period ends the ability to perform the essential functions with that accommodation; the subdivision states that it relieves no one of other accommodation or antidiscrimination obligations and that no employee may be required to waive such rights as a condition of the extension. Government Code section 19173 states the grounds on which a probationer may be rejected during the period — reasons relating to the probationer's qualifications, the good of the service, or failure to demonstrate merit, efficiency, fitness, and moral responsibility — and provides that the probationer may not be rejected for any cause constituting prohibited discrimination as set forth in sections 19700 to 19703. Subdivision (b) prescribes the written notice of rejection, its contents, an effective date no later than the last day of the probationary period, and a filing with the board within fifteen days after that date.

expectedJSON.body: Ferdig v. State Personnel Board is a California Supreme Court decision about an appointment that was made after the appointee was placed in the certified group by a credit he was never entitled to. The appointee passed a Chief Engineer II examination and was ranked sixteenth. He then applied for a veterans' preference on the strength of a discharge document; the Department of Veterans Affairs advised the State Personnel Board that preference points applied, which moved him to fourth, and a waiver by a candidate ahead of him brought him into the top three and so within the group eligible for appointment. He was appointed. The preference was later determined to have been approved erroneously, because his service did not satisfy the statutory service requirement. The Supreme Court held that the appointee had not been entitled at any time to the preference points that made him eligible, stated the principle that an administrative agency's action taken in excess of, or in violation of, the powers conferred on it is void, and concluded that the appointment itself was void and that the board had authority to revoke it from the beginning. The court separately rejected the argument that the expiration of the six-month probationary period insulated the appointment, holding that the probationary-rejection section was not the vehicle by which the separation was effected and was not intended to cure a defect in certification and appointment arising from a violation of the civil service statutes.

As it now reads, it applies where the appointment of an employee has been made and accepted in good faith but would not have been made but for a mistake of law or fact that, if known to the parties, would have rendered the appointment unlawful when made; in that situation the department may declare the appointment void from the beginning if the action is taken within one year after the appointment. expectedJSON.body: The consequence of filling a position by statutory appointment rather than by agreement runs through the whole subject. In Miller v. State of California the California Supreme Court, rejecting a state civil service employee's claim to a vested contractual right to serve until a mandatory retirement age in effect when he was hired, stated the settled rule that public employment in California is not held by contract but by statute, and that so far as the duration of such employment is concerned no employee has a vested contractual right to continue in employment beyond the time or contrary to the terms and conditions fixed by law. The court in the same opinion distinguished pension rights, which it described as deferred compensation earned on the performance of services and protected by the contract clause, from tenure in a civil service position, which it did not. The Supreme Court repeated the Miller sentence, with its page citation, in Cal Fire Local 2881 v. California Public Employees' Retirement System, where it framed contract clause protection of the terms and conditions of public employment as historically the exception rather than the rule.
